For each item return:

Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.

Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

Context: After fine-tuning models on two conflicting traits, the team observed substantial CoT override: the reasoning plans one kind of answer but the response does the opposite (74% for one model, 17% for the other). They knew fine-tuning had disturbed thinking behaviour somewhat, since some rollouts lacked a proper thinking block or an answer and had to be resampled. They had to decide whether this damage could account for the override.
O1: Treat fine-tuning damage as a live explanation and invest further in testing it, e.g. with a battery of CoT-dependence tasks across multiple capability benchmarks, before moving on to other hypotheses.
O2: Report benchmark scores of the fine-tuned model against the base and non-poisoned fine-tuned models, noting a modest drop partly attributable to answer-format mismatch, and conclude that most reasoning ability is retained.
O3: Run a matched control: fine-tune on a single trait only and on a mixed but non-conflicting dataset, and compare override rates to isolate conflict from general fine-tuning damage.
O4: Rejected capability degradation as a sufficient explanation, citing retained GPQA Diamond performance and CoT-following when the same persona answers.
O5: Replay the same CoT prefills on the base model and on checkpoints at several points during fine-tuning, with many samples per item, to see whether override tracks training progress and not just final damage.
